children: The overseas tally compares with approximately USD 349 billion attributed on the same founder-share basis across 102 unicorns based in India, according to a report by Prosus and Dealroom

Founders who grew up in India account for an estimated USD 560 billion in founder-share-attributed value across current and former unicorns headquartered overseas, underscoring the growing global footprint of Indian entrepreneurial talent, according to the Indian Diaspora Index by Prosus and Dealroom.

The figure is indicative rather than a measure of actual founder ownership. Under the index’s methodology, the valuation of each company is divided equally among its founders, with the portion attributable to qualifying Indian-origin founders then counted towards the total, irrespective of their actual shareholding.

The overseas tally compares with approximately USD 349 billion attributed on the same founder-share basis across 102 unicorns based in India. Flipkart, Zomato and Groww account for the largest portions of this domestic value, at USD 36 billion, USD 30 billion and USD 16 billion, respectively.

The index identifies 70 unicorns, collectively valued at USD 243 billion, that were built by all-Indian founding teams. These include companies such as Zscaler, Rubrik, Nutanix and Skild, founded by entrepreneurs including Jay Chaudhry; Arvind Jain, Arvind Nithrakashyap, Bipul Sinha and Soham Mazumdar; Ajeet Singh, Dheeraj Pandey and Mohit Aron; and Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta.

A further 135 unicorns, including Palo Alto, Bloom Energy, Astera Labs and Perplexity, have Indian-origin founders within their core founding teams. Together, these companies contribute another USD 317 billion on the index’s founder-share basis.

The findings point to the scale at which Indian-origin founders have participated in building technology companies beyond the domestic ecosystem, particularly in markets where access to capital, talent and technology infrastructure can support rapid global expansion.

A broader birth-origin analysis in the index places the United States at the centre of this diaspora-led company creation. About 62 per cent of the companies in the broader cohort are based in the US.

Of the 323 companies covered in this analysis, 200 were either started in the US (178) or relocated there (22). The broader analysis, however, differs from the narrower overseas index: it includes founders who left India as children as well as companies based in India.

The index comes as India's startup ecosystem continues to produce founders whose companies extend well beyond the country's borders, with the data highlighting the substantial value attributed to Indian-origin entrepreneurial talent in global technology markets.
